name: Causation
statement: The relation by which one thing brings about another, harder to analyze than it looks.
meaning: Causation is the relation between cause and effect, one thing bringing about, producing, or making a difference to another. The central metaphysical question is what causation is, what the causal relation consists in, and the modern debate begins with David Hume's influential empiricist analysis in his Treatise of Human Nature of 1739 to 1740 and his Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding of 1748. Hume argued that we never observe a necessary connection between cause and effect; all we observe is constant conjunction, that events of one type are regularly followed by events of another, together with temporal priority, the cause coming before the effect, and contiguity. Our idea of necessary connection, he held, is a projection of the mind's habit of expectation, not something read off the objects, and he gave two definitions of cause in these terms. This motivates the regularity theory, on which causation is roughly a matter of constant conjunction with no real necessity in the world. Because naive regularity theory struggles to distinguish genuine causes from mere correlations, later theories offer other analyses: counterfactual theories, on David Lewis's account of 1973, analyze causation as counterfactual dependence, that had the cause not occurred the effect would not have; probabilistic theories hold that causes raise the probability of their effects; process theories, from Salmon and Dowe, appeal to physical processes that transmit a conserved quantity; and manipulability or interventionist theories, from von Wright and Woodward, tie causes to what could be manipulated to change effects. Causation is central to metaphysics, science, and law.
mechanism: Theories of causation try to say what makes it true that one event caused another, and each captures part of the phenomenon while facing characteristic problems. Hume's starting point is that observation reveals only patterns: we see the cue ball strike the eight ball and the eight ball move, and after many such cases we come to expect the second on seeing the first, but we never perceive a further ingredient of necessity binding them; so, for Hume, the necessity we ascribe to causes is a feeling of the mind projected outward, and causation, objectively, reduces to regular succession. The regularity theory formalizes this but cannot by itself separate causes from coincidental regularities or from joint effects of a common cause. Counterfactual theories address this by asking what would have happened otherwise: on Lewis's 1973 account, analyzed through the comparative similarity of possible worlds, an event c causes e when e counterfactually depends on c, that is, had c not occurred, e would not have; to handle cases where a backup cause is waiting, called preemption, and cases of overdetermination, where two sufficient causes act at once, Lewis appealed to chains of stepwise counterfactual dependence. Probabilistic theories, from Reichenbach and Suppes, suit indeterministic causation by requiring that a cause raise the probability of its effect. Process theories, from Wesley Salmon and Phil Dowe, distinguish genuine causal processes, which transmit a conserved quantity or a mark, from mere pseudo-processes like a moving shadow. Manipulability and interventionist theories, from von Wright and James Woodward, and causal-modeling approaches using structural equations, associated with Judea Pearl, analyze causes as factors one could in principle intervene on to bring about changes in their effects.

examples.text: Hume held we observe only regular succession, not a necessary connection, so our idea of necessity is a habit of the mind.
On Lewis's theory, c causes e if, had c not occurred, e would not have occurred, analyzed through nearby possible worlds.
Salmon and Dowe distinguish causal processes that transmit a conserved quantity from pseudo-processes like a moving shadow.

variants.name: Regularity and counterfactual theories
variants.text: Hume's constant-conjunction account, and Lewis's analysis of causation as counterfactual dependence between events.

variants.name: Process and interventionist theories
variants.text: Salmon and Dowe's conserved-quantity processes, and Woodward's account of causes as targets of intervention.

whyItMatters: Causation is one of the most fundamental relations there is, woven into science, everyday reasoning, and the law, and getting clear about it is a central task of metaphysics. Science is in large part the search for causes, and the difference between finding a genuine cause and merely noting a correlation, captured in the maxim that correlation is not causation, is crucial to medicine, economics, and every experimental discipline. The law turns on causation in assigning responsibility, asking whether a defendant's act caused a harm. And ordinary explanation, prediction, and control all depend on tracking what brings about what. Hume's analysis reframed the whole subject by challenging the assumption that we perceive necessary connections in nature, and his problem, of saying what more there is to causation than regular succession, has driven philosophy ever since, generating the counterfactual, probabilistic, process, and interventionist theories that structure the modern debate. The puzzles causation raises, about its direction and asymmetry, about preemption and overdetermination, and about causation by absence, continue to test every theory. As the relation by which the world hangs together across time, and the relation on which explanation, responsibility, and control depend, causation is a foundational topic in metaphysics and the philosophy of science.

working.text: take causation as the relation by which one event brings about or makes a difference to another.
spell it out as regularity, counterfactual dependence, probability-raising, a physical process, or manipulability.
check the analysis against preemption, overdetermination, and the difference between causes and correlations.

limits: No analysis of causation commands consensus, and each of the main theories faces well-known counterexamples. The regularity theory cannot by itself distinguish a genuine cause from an accidental regularity or from a joint effect of a common cause, and it struggles with single-case causation. Counterfactual theories handle many cases elegantly but face persistent trouble with preemption, where a backup cause stands ready so that the effect would still have occurred even without the actual cause, and with overdetermination, where two sufficient causes operate together; Lewis's appeals to chains of dependence and later refinements remain disputed. Probabilistic theories must say how probability-raising relates to actual causation and confront cases where a cause lowers the probability of its effect. Process theories must specify which quantities and processes count and how to treat causation by absence or omission, where nothing physical is transmitted. The direction and asymmetry of causation, why causes precede effects, is itself a deep problem. Some details reward care: Hume's works span 1739 to 1748, Lewis's Causation is dated 1973, and attributions to Reichenbach, Suppes, Salmon, Dowe, von Wright, Woodward, and Pearl reward checking. So causation robustly names the relation by which one thing brings about another, understood as a phenomenon whose correct analysis remains contested across the regularity, counterfactual, probabilistic, process, and interventionist theories.
misreadings: Causation is not the same as correlation; two things can be regularly associated without one causing the other, as when both are effects of a common cause. Hume's analysis is not the claim that there is no causation, but that its objective content is regular succession rather than a perceived necessary connection. And counterfactual dependence is not simply identical to causation, since preemption and overdetermination show effects can occur without depending counterfactually on their actual causes, so treating causation as mere correlation, as denied by Hume, or as plain counterfactual dependence, misreads the topic.
origin: The metaphysical study of the cause-effect relation, reframed by Hume's regularity analysis in 1739 to 1748 and developed through the counterfactual, probabilistic, process, and interventionist theories of Lewis, Salmon, Woodward, and others.

sources.text: The Metaphysics of Causation, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — the central question of what the causal relation consists in, token and type causation, and the range of theories including regularity, counterfactual, probabilistic, process, and manipulability accounts, with the problems of preemption and overdetermination.

Counterfactual Theories of Causation, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Lewis's 1973 analysis of causation as counterfactual dependence via possible-world similarity, the treatment of preemption and overdetermination through chains of dependence, and Hume's counterfactual-flavored second definition.
